f: In March 2012 Greece swapped its privately held bonds at a loss of more than half their face value: the biggest sovereign restructuring in history.
q: The marked point is the peak of the Greek debt crisis, just before the biggest sovereign restructuring in history.

f: In November 2011 Italy's 10-year yield averaged 7.06%. Silvio Berlusconi resigned as prime minister that same month.
q: The marked point is the month Italy's yield passed 7% and its prime minister resigned.

f: Spain's 10-year yield averaged 6.79% in July 2012, the month Mario Draghi promised to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro.
q: The marked point is the month Mario Draghi promised to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro.

f: Portugal asked for an EU-IMF bailout in April 2011. Its 10-year yield peaked at 13.85% in January 2012.
q: The marked point is the peak after Portugal's EU-IMF bailout.

f: Ireland's banking collapse ended in an €85bn EU-IMF rescue in November 2010. Its yield peaked at 12.45% in July 2011.
q: The marked point is the peak after Ireland's €85bn rescue.

f: Paul Volcker's Fed squeezed out inflation with record interest rates. The 10-year Treasury averaged 15.32% in September 1981, its all-time high.
q: The Fed squeezed out inflation with record interest rates, and the 10-year Treasury hit its all-time high.

f: On 16 September 1992, "Black Wednesday", the pound crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
q: The pound crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, on a day traders still call Black Wednesday.

f: In September 1992 Sweden's central bank raised its overnight rate to 500% to defend the krona. It let the currency float two months later.
q: The central bank raised its overnight rate to 500% to defend the krona. Two months later it gave up and let the currency float.

f: In September 1992 the lira was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, the same week as the pound.
The Fed's surprise hikes in 1994 caused the "great bond massacre": the 10-year Treasury went from 5.75% in January to 7.96% in November.
q: Surprise Fed rate hikes set off what traders called the great bond massacre.

f: The Bank of Japan announced negative interest rates in January 2016, effective in February. That month Japan's 10-year yield averaged below zero for the first time.
q: The marked point is the first month Japan's 10-year yield averaged below zero.

f: Japan's asset bubble burst in 1990. Its 10-year yield peaked at 8.03% in September 1990, then began a decades-long slide.
q: The asset bubble burst. The yield peaked here, then began a slide that lasted decades.

f: In January 2015 the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap on the franc. Swiss 10-year yields were negative in 59 of the 72 months from 2015 to 2020.
q: The central bank scrapped its cap on the franc without warning.

f: Germany's 10-year yield first averaged below zero in June 2016, the month of the Brexit vote.
q: The marked point is the first month Germany's 10-year yield averaged below zero: the month of the Brexit vote.

f: The September 2022 "mini-budget" set off a gilt sell-off: the 10-year yield jumped from 2.33% in August to 3.50% in September, and the Bank of England stepped in.
q: The marked point is the gilt sell-off after the "mini-budget".

f: In March 2020 the 10-year Treasury averaged below 1% for the first time, at 0.87%.
q: The marked point is the first month the 10-year Treasury averaged below 1%.

f: In October 2023 the 10-year Treasury averaged 4.80%, its highest monthly level since July 2007.
q: The marked point is the 10-year Treasury's highest monthly level since July 2007.

f: After François Mitterrand won the presidency in May 1981, capital fled France and its 10-year yield passed 17%.
q: A new Socialist president took office, and capital fled the country.

f: A currency crisis after New Zealand's 1984 snap election led to sweeping free-market reforms. Its yield peaked at 18.71% in May 1985.
q: A currency crisis after a snap election led to sweeping free-market reforms.

f: In September 1985 South Africa froze repayments on its foreign debt after banks pulled their credit lines.
The 1998 emerging-market crisis hit the rand hard. South Africa's 10-year yield averaged 18.30% in September 1998.
q: The marked point is the peak of an emerging-market rout that hit the rand.

f: Canadian rates followed the Fed up. Canada's 10-year yield peaked at 17.00% in September 1981.
q: The marked point is Canada's peak, as rates followed the Fed up.

f: Hungarian inflation passed 25% in early 2023, among the highest in the EU. Its 10-year yield peaked at 10.25% in October 2022.
q: The marked point is the peak of Hungary's inflation shock.

f: Poland joined the EU in 2004. Its 10-year yield fell from 11.86% in August 2001 to 4.72% in July 2005.
Greece adopted the euro in January 2001. By mid-2003 its 10-year yield was within 0.2 points of Germany's.
Italy's 10-year yield fell from 13.45% in March 1995 to below 5% by July 1998 as it raced to qualify for the euro.
In 1976 Britain borrowed $3.9bn from the IMF, then the largest loan the fund had ever made.
q: Britain borrowed $3.9bn from the IMF, then the largest loan the fund had ever made.

f: Ireland's 1980s debt crisis pushed its 10-year yield to 19.47% in February 1982.
q: The marked point is the peak of Ireland's 1980s debt crisis.

f: Oil prices collapsed in 1986 and hit Norway hard: the krone was devalued by 12% in May 1986.
A banking crisis and the collapse of Soviet trade sank Finland's economy in 1991. The markka was floated in September 1992.
During the second intifada and a sliding shekel, Israel's 10-year yield reached 11.67% in October 2002. It peaked at 11.69% in February 2003.
q: The marked point is Israel's squeeze during the second intifada.

f: The 2008 financial crisis pushed Mexico's 10-year yield to 9.82% in November 2008.
q: The marked point is Mexico's yield during the global financial crisis.

f: Chile's 2019 protests were followed by pension-fund withdrawals. Its 10-year yield rose from 2.70% in August 2019 to 6.34% in October 2021.
q: The marked point is the peak after Chile's pension-fund withdrawals.

f: Slovenia's yield peaked at 6.90% in December 2011. In 2013 it rescued its own banks and narrowly avoided an EU bailout.
q: The marked point is Slovenia's peak during the euro crisis.

f: Australia floated its dollar in December 1983, ending decades of a managed exchange rate.
Inflation rose with the Vietnam War. In August 1971 Richard Nixon ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.
q: The president ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.

f: The 1973 oil shock pushed German 10-year yields above 10% in 1974, peaking at 10.8%.
q: The marked point is Germany's peak after the first oil shock.

t: The franc as a safe haven
f: Money poured into the franc in the late 1970s. In October 1978 the Swiss National Bank set a floor against the Deutsche Mark.
q: The marked point is the low as money poured into the Swiss franc.

f: Spain devalued the peseta three times between September 1992 and May 1993.
Belgium's public debt passed 100% of GDP in the 1980s, one of the highest levels in Europe.
In autumn 1982 Denmark fixed its exchange rate, banned wage indexation and tightened its budget. Long-term yields fell from 23.22% in September 1982 to 14.19% by April 1983.
q: The government fixed the exchange rate, banned wage indexation and slashed the deficit, and yields fell by 9 points in seven months.

f: In July 2012 Denmark's central bank became one of the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.
q: The central bank became one of the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.

f: In 1981 the Bank of Italy stopped having to buy the government bonds the Treasury could not sell, the so-called divorce. From then on the market set the price.
q: The central bank stopped having to buy the bonds the Treasury couldn't sell, the so-called "divorce."

f: In November 2016 Donald Trump's election win set off a bond sell-off. The 10-year Treasury rose from 1.76% in October to 2.49% in December.
q: A surprise presidential election result set off a bond sell-off.

f: In October 1979 Fed chair Paul Volcker announced, at a rare Saturday press conference, that the Fed would target the money supply. The 10-year yield jumped from 9.33% to 10.30% in a month.
q: A new Fed chair announced a radical policy shift at a rare Saturday press conference.

f: Greece held two elections in six weeks, in May and June 2012, with leaving the euro openly debated. Its 10-year yield climbed back to 27.82% in June 2012.
q: Two elections in six weeks, with leaving the euro openly debated.

f: In January 2015 the anti-austerity party Syriza won a snap election. In July 2015 voters rejected the bailout terms in a referendum. Greece's 10-year yield rose from 8.42% in December 2014 to 12.00% in April 2015.
q: An anti-austerity party won a snap election. Months later, voters rejected the bailout terms in a referendum.

f: Italy's new populist coalition took office in June 2018. That October the European Commission rejected its draft budget, a first for any member state, and Italy's spread over Germany reached 3.07 points.
q: A new populist coalition clashed with Brussels, and the European Commission rejected Italy's draft budget, a first for any member state.

f: On June 23, 2016, British voters chose to leave the EU. In August the Bank of England cut rates and restarted bond buying, and the 10-year gilt yield fell to 0.74%.
q: Voters chose to leave the EU. The Bank of England cut rates and restarted bond buying.

f: In May 1997, in its first week in office, the new Labour government handed control of interest rates to the Bank of England. The 10-year gilt yield fell from 7.64% in April to 7.17% in May.
q: In its first week, a new government handed control of interest rates to the Bank of England.

f: In October 1979 the new Conservative government abolished exchange controls that had been in place since 1939. The 10-year gilt yield rose from 13.09% that month to 14.76% in November.
q: The new government abolished exchange controls that had been in place for 40 years.

t: Three finance ministers in a week
f: In December 2015 President Jacob Zuma fired his finance minister. Within a week South Africa had had three, and its 10-year yield rose from 8.49% in November to 9.63% in January.
q: The president fired the finance minister, and within a week the country had had three.

f: In February 1990 Chancellor Helmut Kohl offered East Germany a monetary union, months before reunification. Germany's 10-year yield jumped from 7.70% in January to 8.57% in February.
q: The chancellor offered East Germany a monetary union, ahead of reunification.

f: In January 1995, with Canada's 10-year yield above 9%, a Wall Street Journal editorial called the country an honorary member of the Third World. The next month's federal budget began deep spending cuts.
q: With yields above 9%, a Wall Street Journal editorial called the country an honorary member of the Third World. A deficit-cutting budget followed.

f: In June 2024 President Emmanuel Macron called a snap election. In December 2024 the government fell in the first successful no-confidence vote since 1962. France's spread over Germany widened from 0.51 points in May to 0.83 in December.
q: The president called a snap election. Six months later, the government fell in the first successful no-confidence vote since 1962.

f: In April 2013 the Bank of Japan promised to double the money base in two years. Japan's 10-year yield dipped to 0.49% that month, then jumped to 0.88% in May.
q: The central bank promised to double the money supply in two years.

f: In 1994 a global bond rout met a Swedish budget deficit of over 10% of GDP. Sweden's 10-year yield rose from 6.84% in January to 11.24% in September.
q: A global bond rout and a budget deficit of over 10% of GDP.

f: In May and June 2013 Fed chair Ben Bernanke signaled that the Fed could slow its bond buying. The "taper tantrum" sent the 10-year Treasury from 1.76% in April to 2.81% in September.
q: The central bank hinted it might slow its bond buying, and traders threw what became known as a tantrum.

f: In December 2008 the Fed cut its policy rate to near zero for the first time. The 10-year Treasury fell from 3.53% in November to 2.42%.
q: The central bank cut its policy rate to near zero for the first time.

f: In August 2011 S&P cut the US credit rating from AAA for the first time. Investors bought Treasuries anyway: the 10-year yield fell from 3.00% in July to 1.98% in September.
q: A rating agency took away the country's top credit rating for the first time, and yields fell anyway.

f: On October 19, 1987, Black Monday, the Dow Jones fell 22.6% in a single day. The 10-year Treasury, at 9.52% that month, fell to 8.86% in November.
q: The stock market had its worst day ever, losing more than a fifth of its value in one session.

f: In September 1998 the New York Fed organized a rescue of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management. The 10-year Treasury fell to 4.53% in October.
q: A giant hedge fund collapsed, and the central bank organized its rescue by Wall Street banks.

f: In 2022 the Fed raised rates faster than at any time since the early 1980s. The 10-year Treasury reached 3.98% in October 2022, up from 1.58% a year earlier.
q: The central bank was raising rates at its fastest pace in four decades.

f: In March 1980 President Jimmy Carter imposed credit controls to fight inflation. The 10-year Treasury peaked at 12.75% that month, then fell to 9.78% by June.
q: The president imposed controls on credit to fight inflation.

f: In August 2019 Germany's 10-year yield averaged -0.65%, its lowest ever: investors were paying to lend to the government.
q: Investors paid the government more than ever before to lend it money for 10 years.

f: In July 1992 the Bundesbank raised its discount rate to 8.75%, the highest since 1931. Weeks later Europe's exchange-rate system was in crisis.
q: The central bank raised its discount rate to the highest in six decades, and Europe's currency grid started to crack.

f: Germany's 10-year yield fell to 0.12% in April 2015, weeks after the ECB began buying government bonds, then jumped to 0.79% by June in the "Bund tantrum."
q: Weeks after the central bank began buying government bonds, the yield nearly hit zero, then spiked.

f: In March 1983 President François Mitterrand chose to keep the franc in the European Monetary System and turned to austerity, the "tournant de la rigueur."
q: The Socialist government dropped its spending program and turned to austerity to defend the currency.

f: On August 2, 1993, after speculators attacked the franc, Europe's exchange-rate bands were widened to 15% either side. France's 10-year yield fell from 6.75% in July to 5.98% in October.
q: After speculators attacked the currency, Europe's exchange-rate bands were widened to 15% either side.

f: On September 20, 1992, French voters approved the Maastricht Treaty with 51% of the vote.
q: Voters approved a new European treaty by just 51%.

f: In May 1968 student protests and a general strike brought France to a standstill. Capital fled, and the franc came under heavy pressure that autumn.
q: Student protests and a nationwide general strike brought the country to a standstill.

f: In July 1992 Italy's government took 0.6% from every bank account overnight to help cut the deficit. Two months later the lira left the ERM.
q: The government took 0.6% out of every bank account overnight.

f: In July 2022 Mario Draghi resigned as prime minister after his coalition fell apart. Italy's 10-year yield rose from 3.36% that month to 4.53% in October.
q: The prime minister, a former central banker, resigned after his coalition fell apart.

f: In May 2010 Greece agreed a €110 billion bailout with the EU and the IMF, the first of three. Its 10-year yield still rose from 7.97% that month to 10.70% by August.
q: The country agreed the first of three EU-IMF bailouts.

f: On September 30, 2008, Ireland guaranteed the deposits and debts of its six main banks, about €440 billion.
q: The government guaranteed the deposits and debts of its six main banks overnight.

f: In August 1986 Ireland devalued its currency, the punt, by 8% within the European Monetary System. Its 10-year yield rose from 10.96% that month to 13.90% by October.
q: The currency was devalued by 8%, and yields jumped by 3 points in two months.

f: In November 1967 Britain devalued the pound by 14%, from $2.80 to $2.40. Prime Minister Harold Wilson said the "pound in your pocket" had not been devalued.
q: The pound was devalued by 14%, and the prime minister said the "pound in your pocket" was unaffected.

f: In October 1990 Britain joined the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. It left on Black Wednesday, less than two years later.
q: The country finally joined Europe's exchange-rate system, and would crash out of it within two years.

f: In March 2009 the Bank of England cut its rate to 0.5%, the lowest in its 315-year history, and began buying gilts with newly created money.
q: The central bank cut rates to the lowest in its 300-year history and started creating money to buy bonds.

t: The SNB's first hike in 15 years
f: In June 2022 the Swiss National Bank raised rates for the first time in 15 years. The 10-year yield reached 1.15% that month, from -0.13% at the end of 2021.
q: The central bank raised rates for the first time in 15 years.

f: In July 2009 Sweden's central bank cut its deposit rate to -0.25%, the first central bank in the world to go below zero.
q: The central bank became the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.

f: In December 1992 Norway let the krone float after a speculative attack. Its 10-year yield fell from 9.42% that month to 7.67% by March 1993.
q: After a speculative attack, the central bank gave up its currency peg and let it float.

f: In November 1991, in the middle of a deep depression, Finland devalued the markka by 12.3%.
q: In the middle of a deep depression, the currency was devalued by 12%.

f: On June 2, 1992, Danish voters rejected the Maastricht Treaty with 50.7% of the vote, shaking Europe's currency markets.
q: Voters narrowly rejected a new European treaty.

f: In December 1998 the finance ministry's Trust Fund Bureau said it would stop buying government bonds. Japan's 10-year yield jumped from 0.88% in October to 2.12% in February 1999.
q: A huge government fund said it would stop buying government bonds, and the yield more than doubled in four months.

f: In June 2003 Japan's 10-year yield fell to 0.53%, a record low at the time, then nearly tripled to 1.41% by August as banks sold bonds.
q: The yield fell to a record low, then nearly tripled within two months as banks dumped bonds.

f: In December 2022 the Bank of Japan unexpectedly let its 10-year yield cap rise from 0.25% to 0.5%.
q: The central bank unexpectedly loosened the cap it held on the 10-year yield.

f: In March 2024 the Bank of Japan ended eight years of negative interest rates with its first hike in 17 years. The 10-year yield rose from 0.72% that month to 1.07% in May.
q: The central bank ended eight years of negative rates with its first hike in 17 years.

f: In March 1990 New Zealand's central bank signed the world's first formal inflation target, 0 to 2% by 1992. Dozens of countries later copied the model.
q: The central bank became the first in the world to work to a formal inflation target.

f: At the end of March 2017 President Jacob Zuma fired finance minister Pravin Gordhan. Days later S&P cut South Africa's foreign-currency rating to junk.
q: The president fired a respected finance minister, and a rating agency cut the country to junk days later.

f: In October 2008 Hungary became the first EU country to get an IMF rescue in the financial crisis, a $25 billion package with the EU and the World Bank. Its 10-year yield jumped from 7.99% in September to 9.57%.
q: It became the first EU country of the financial crisis to need an IMF rescue.

f: On December 16, 2014, as the ruble collapsed, Russia's central bank raised its key rate from 10.5% to 17% overnight.
q: With the currency collapsing, the central bank raised its key rate from 10.5% to 17% overnight.

f: In June 2022 the Czech National Bank raised its main rate to 7%, the highest since 1999. The 10-year yield reached 5.12% that month.
q: The central bank raised its main rate to the highest level in more than 20 years.

f: In February 1982 Belgium devalued its franc by 8.5%, its first devaluation in more than 30 years, and changed its wage indexation.
q: The currency was devalued for the first time in more than 30 years.

f: In March 2020 the Reserve Bank of Australia began targeting the 3-year bond yield at 0.25%, a first for the country.
q: The central bank started targeting a government bond yield directly, as Japan did.

f: In August 2013 the rupee hit a record low as investors fled emerging markets after the Fed's taper talk. India's 10-year yield rose from 7.40% in June to 8.86% in November.
q: Talk of tighter money in America sent the currency to a record low.

f: In November 2016 the peso tumbled after Donald Trump, who had promised to renegotiate NAFTA, won the US election. Mexico's 10-year yield rose from 6.09% in October to 7.60% in January.
q: An election result abroad sent the currency tumbling.

f: On March 23, 2011, Portugal's parliament rejected the government's austerity plan and Prime Minister José Sócrates resigned. Two weeks later Portugal asked for a bailout.
q: Parliament rejected an austerity plan, the prime minister resigned, and a bailout request followed within weeks.

f: In December 2008 Latvia agreed a €7.5 billion rescue from the EU, the IMF, its Nordic neighbors and others. Its economy shrank by about 14% in 2009.
q: The country agreed a €7.5 billion rescue from the EU, the IMF and its Nordic neighbors.

f: On 1 September 1998 Malaysia imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, rather than turn to the IMF.
q: The government imposed capital controls and pegged the currency, rather than turn to the IMF.
